title: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Food
summary: How green plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make their own sugary food in their leaves, giving off the oxygen that people and animals breathe.
poll: Plants are the most important living things on Earth.

versions.title: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
You eat food. A plant does not eat. It makes its own food!

A plant needs three things. It needs sunlight. It needs water. It needs a gas from the air.

The roots take in the water. The water goes up the stem. It goes to each leaf.

The gas gets in through tiny holes. The holes are on the leaf. You can not see them.

Leaves are green. They have green stuff in them. It is called chlorophyll. It soaks up the sun.

The leaf uses the light. It mixes the gas and the water. Now it has sugar! The sugar is food. It helps the plant grow.

The plant lets out a gas too. It is oxygen. We need it to breathe. So plants help us live!

In Saudi Arabia, date palms do this. The sun is hot and bright. The palms make sweet dates.

versions.title: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
You eat food to grow. But a plant does not eat at all. It makes its own food.

A plant needs three things to make food. It needs sunlight. It needs water. It needs a gas from the air.

The roots take in water from the soil. The water moves up the stem. Then it goes into each leaf.

The gas comes in through tiny holes in the leaf. The holes are too small to see.

Leaves look green. That is because they hold a green stuff called chlorophyll. It soaks up sunlight like a sponge.

The leaf uses the light to mix the water and the gas. This makes sugar. The sugar is food for the plant. It helps the plant grow tall and strong.

As it works, the plant lets out a gas called oxygen. People and animals need oxygen to breathe. So plants help keep us alive.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms make food this way. They use the bright desert sun. Then they store the sugar in sweet dates.

versions.title: Plants Make Their Own Food
versions.text:
When you are hungry, you get a snack. A plant cannot walk to find food. So it makes its own food in its leaves.

A plant needs three things to make food. It needs sunlight and water. It also needs a gas from the air. This gas is called carbon dioxide.

The roots pull up water from the soil. The water goes up the stem and into the leaves.

The gas gets in through tiny holes on each leaf. The holes are much too small to see.

Leaves are green because they are full of chlorophyll. This green stuff soaks up the energy in sunlight.

The leaf uses that energy to join the water and the gas. Together they make a kind of sugar. The sugar is the plant's food. The plant uses it to grow new leaves, stems, roots, and fruit.

While it makes sugar, the plant gives off oxygen. People and animals breathe in oxygen to stay alive. So each green plant helps us.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow in the hot desert sun. They make sugar in their long leaves. They store it in sweet, sticky dates.

versions.title: Plants Make Their Own Food
versions.text:
When you feel hungry, you can grab a snack. A plant cannot move around to find a meal. So it makes its own food in its leaves. It does this each sunny day.

To make food, a plant needs three things. It needs sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air around us.

The roots soak up water from the soil. Thin tubes carry the water up the stem and into the leaves.

Carbon dioxide gets into the leaf through tiny holes on its surface. They are so small that you need a microscope to see them.

Leaves look green because they hold chlorophyll. This green stuff soaks up the energy in sunlight very well.

The leaf uses this energy to join the water and the carbon dioxide. The result is a kind of sugar. The sugar is the plant's food. It gives the plant the energy to grow new leaves, stems, roots, flowers, and fruit.

As the plant makes sugar, it lets oxygen out into the air. People and animals need oxygen to breathe, so green plants help keep us all alive.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow well under the hot desert sun. They make sugar in their long leaves. Then they store much of it in their sweet, sticky dates.

versions.title: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
When you feel hungry, you can go to the kitchen and find a snack. A plant cannot move to find a meal, so it does something amazing instead. It makes its own food inside its leaves, and this is called photosynthesis. The word means "putting together with light."

A plant needs three things for photosynthesis. It needs sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a gas that people and animals breathe out into the air.

The roots soak up water from the soil. Thin tubes carry it up the stem to the leaves. Carbon dioxide gets into each leaf through tiny holes called stomata, which are too small to see without a microscope.

Leaves are green because they hold chlorophyll. This green stuff is very good at trapping the energy in sunlight.

The leaf uses that energy to join the water and the carbon dioxide. This makes a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose is the plant's food. It gives the plant energy, and it is also used to build new leaves, stems, roots, and fruit.

A plant does not use all of its glucose at once. It saves some for later and may store it in its roots, seeds, or fruit.

Photosynthesis also makes oxygen. The plant lets it out through its stomata. People and animals need oxygen to breathe, so green plants help keep the air good for all of us.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow well in the hot desert sun. They make glucose in their long leaves and store much of it as sugar in their sweet dates.

versions.title: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
When you feel hungry, you can walk into the kitchen and choose something to eat. A plant, however, cannot wander around in search of a meal, so it does something remarkable instead: it makes its own food inside its leaves. Scientists call this process photosynthesis, a word that comes from Greek and means "putting together with light."

Photosynthesis requires three ingredients, which are sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is an invisible gas that people and animals breathe out into the air every time they exhale.

The roots absorb water from the soil, and narrow tubes carry it up through the stem to the leaves. At the same time, carbon dioxide enters each leaf through tiny openings called stomata, which the plant can open and close when it needs to.

Leaves look green because they contain a pigment called chlorophyll, which is especially good at capturing the energy in sunlight.

The leaf uses this captured energy to combine water and carbon dioxide, and the result is a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose is the plant's food, which it uses both as a source of energy and as building material for new leaves, stems, roots, flowers, and fruit.

A plant does not use all of its glucose right away. Instead, it saves some for later, storing it in its roots, seeds, or fruit until the plant needs the extra energy.

Photosynthesis also produces oxygen, which the plant releases through its stomata. Because people and animals depend on oxygen to breathe, green plants help keep the air healthy for every living creature on Earth.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms grow well under the strong desert sunshine. They make glucose in their long, feathery leaves and store a large amount of it as sugar in their sweet, sticky dates.

versions.title: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
When you feel hungry, you can walk into the kitchen and choose something to eat. A plant, however, cannot wander around in search of a meal, so it does something remarkable instead: it makes its own food inside its leaves. Scientists call this process photosynthesis, a word that comes from Greek and means "putting together with light."

Photosynthesis requires three ingredients, which are sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, an invisible gas that people and animals release into the air every time they breathe out.

The roots absorb water from the surrounding soil, and an intricate network of narrow tubes transports it up through the stem to the leaves. At the same time, carbon dioxide enters each leaf through tiny pores called stomata, which the plant can open and close as the weather changes.

Inside the cells of the leaf are tiny structures called chloroplasts, and this is where photosynthesis actually takes place. Chloroplasts contain a green pigment called chlorophyll, which is especially effective at absorbing the red and blue portions of sunlight while reflecting the green, and this reflected light is the reason leaves appear green to our eyes.

The plant uses this absorbed energy to combine water and carbon dioxide, and the result is a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose is the plant's food, which it uses both as a source of energy and as building material for new leaves, stems, roots, flowers, and fruit.

A plant does not use all of its glucose right away. Instead, it stores some for later in its roots, seeds, or fruit, so that it has extra energy when it needs to grow quickly or when sunlight is scarce.

Photosynthesis also produces oxygen as a byproduct, which the plant releases through its stomata. Because plants make their own food, scientists call them producers. Animals, including people, are unable to manufacture their own food, so ultimately they depend on plants both for nourishment and for the oxygen they breathe.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms flourish under the intense desert sunshine, where they produce glucose in their long, feathery leaves and store a considerable amount of it as sugar in their sweet, sticky dates.

versions.text:

A plant, however, is unable to wander in search of a meal, so it accomplishes something extraordinary instead: it manufactures its own nourishment within its leaves. versions.title: Photosynthesis: How Plants Make Food
versions.text:
When you feel hungry, you can simply walk into the kitchen and select something to eat. A plant, however, is incapable of wandering in search of a meal, so it accomplishes something extraordinary instead: it manufactures its own nourishment within its leaves. Scientists call this process photosynthesis, a term derived from Greek that translates approximately as "putting together with light."

Photosynthesis requires three essential ingredients, specifically sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, an invisible gas that animals, including humans, continuously release into the atmosphere whenever they exhale.

The roots absorb water from the surrounding soil, and an intricate network of microscopic vessels transports it upward through the stem to the leaves. Simultaneously, carbon dioxide diffuses into each leaf through minuscule pores called stomata, which the plant regulates by opening and closing them in response to fluctuating environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity.

Within the leaf cells are countless microscopic structures called chloroplasts, where photosynthesis actually occurs. Chloroplasts contain a green pigment called chlorophyll, which is exceptionally efficient at absorbing the red and blue wavelengths of sunlight while reflecting the green wavelengths, and this reflected light explains why foliage appears green to human observers. Many leaves are also broad and flat, an arrangement that maximizes the surface area available for intercepting sunlight.

The plant harnesses this absorbed energy to combine water and carbon dioxide, thereby synthesizing a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose constitutes the plant's food, which it utilizes both as an energy source and as raw material for constructing additional leaves, stems, roots, flowers, and fruit.

A plant does not consume all of its glucose immediately. Instead, it stores a portion in its roots, seeds, or fruit, which guarantees that additional energy will be available whenever the plant must grow rapidly or whenever sunlight becomes temporarily scarce.

Photosynthesis additionally generates oxygen as a byproduct, which the plant releases through its stomata. Because plants manufacture their own nourishment, biologists classify them as producers, whereas animals, including humans, are incapable of producing their own food and consequently depend on plants both for nutrition and for the oxygen they breathe.

In Saudi Arabia, date palms flourish under the intense desert sunshine, producing glucose in their elongated, feathery leaves and storing a considerable proportion of it as concentrated sugar in their exceptionally sweet fruit.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to plant a garden at school
How plants make their own food
Why some plants have no leaves
How farmers pick dates
questions.why: The whole article explains how a plant uses sunlight, water, and a gas from the air to make its own food.

wrong.A: The article does not tell how to plant a garden.
wrong.C: The article is about leaves, not plants without leaves.
wrong.D: Dates are named at the end, but picking them is not the topic.

questions.stem: Which part of the plant takes in water from the soil?
options: The leaves
The flowers
The stem
The roots
questions.why: The article says the roots take in water from the soil.

wrong.A: The water ends up in the leaves, but the roots take it in.
wrong.B: The article does not say flowers take in water.
wrong.C: The water moves up the stem, but the stem does not take it from the soil.

questions.stem: What gas does a plant let out into the air?
options: Oxygen
Smoke
Steam from the sun
Dust
questions.why: The article says that as the plant makes food, it lets out oxygen.

wrong.C: The article does not talk about steam.
wrong.D: Dust is not a gas the plant gives off.

questions.stem: The article says chlorophyll soaks up the sun's light. What does "soaks up" mean here?
options: Makes wet
Takes in
Pushes away
Hides from
questions.why: Chlorophyll takes in the light so the leaf can use it to make food.

wrong.A: Light does not get wet, so the words do not mean "makes wet" here.
wrong.C: Chlorophyll uses the light. It does not push it away.
wrong.D: Chlorophyll does not hide from the sun. It needs the light.

questions.stem: What does the leaf make when it uses light to mix water and the gas?
options: Soil
Rain
Sugar
Seeds of sand
questions.why: The article says mixing the water and the gas with light makes sugar, which is the plant's food.

wrong.A: Soil is in the ground. The leaf does not make it.
wrong.B: Rain falls from clouds. Leaves do not make it.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about sand seeds.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to a plant kept in a dark box for many weeks?
options: It would grow faster than ever.
It would make more oxygen.
Its leaves would turn bright red.
It could not make enough food.
questions.why: A plant needs sunlight to make food. With no light, it could not make the sugar it needs.

wrong.A: Without light, the plant cannot make food to grow.
wrong.B: The plant makes oxygen while it makes food, and it needs light for that.
wrong.C: The article does not say leaves turn red in the dark.

questions.stem: Why does the author say that plants help keep people and animals alive?
options: Plants give off oxygen, and we need it to breathe.
Plants keep the sun from getting too hot.
Plants tell people when it will rain.
Plants drink up all the dirty water.
questions.why: The article explains that plants let out oxygen and that people and animals need oxygen to breathe.

wrong.B: Plants use sunlight, but they do not cool the sun.
wrong.C: The article does not say plants can tell the weather.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about dirty water.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about date palms at the end?
options: To give a list of fruits to buy
To show that palms do not need sun
To give a real example from Saudi Arabia
To explain how to cook dates
questions.why: Date palms are a real example of plants in Saudi Arabia that make food from sunlight and store it in their dates.

wrong.A: The article is not a shopping list.
wrong.B: The article says palms grow in the hot, bright sun, so they do need it.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about cooking.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

wrong.C: Date palms are one example; the article says other plants store glucose too.

wrong.B: The article does not say light joins roots and stems.

As a comparison of plants and animals

questions.stem: On a very hot, dry day, a plant closes many of its stomata to save water. What is the most likely effect on photosynthesis?
options: It would speed up because the leaf stays cooler in the shade.
It would slow down because less carbon dioxide can enter the leaf.
It would stop producing glucose and start producing water.
It would not change at all, because stomata only release oxygen.
questions.why: Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata, so closing them limits an ingredient photosynthesis needs.

wrong.A: The article does not connect closing stomata with faster photosynthesis.
wrong.C: Plants do not switch to producing water.
wrong.D: Stomata also let carbon dioxide in, so closing them matters.

questions.stem: A plant has stored glucose in its roots. Why might this help it during a few weeks of cloudy weather?
options: Stored glucose turns into sunlight.
The roots can photosynthesize in the dark.
It can use the stored energy while it makes less food.
Cloudy weather makes the plant need no energy.
questions.why: The article says plants store glucose so they have extra energy when sunlight is scarce, as it would be in cloudy weather.

wrong.A: Glucose is a sugar; it cannot become light.
wrong.B: Photosynthesis needs light and happens in leaf chloroplasts.
wrong.D: Plants always need energy to live and grow.

questions.stem: How are plants and animals different, according to the article?
options: Plants breathe out carbon dioxide, but animals breathe out oxygen.
Animals have chloroplasts, but plants do not.
Plants need water, but animals do not.
Plants can make their own food, but animals cannot.
questions.why: The article says plants are producers that manufacture food, while animals, including humans, cannot and depend on plants.

wrong.A: The gases are reversed: plants release oxygen, and animals exhale carbon dioxide.
wrong.B: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells.
wrong.C: The article never says animals do not need water.

HIGH.prompt: The author says animals "ultimately depend" on plants. Explain this claim, using evidence about both food and oxygen from the article.
checklist: I explained the claim in my own words.
I used evidence about both food and oxygen.
I organized my answer with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
